when-should-a-child-start-reading:
There is no age at which reading starts. There is a long build-up in which nothing looks like reading, and then a few months in which it suddenly does. Most of the worry parents carry is about the build-up, mistaken for a delay.

What follows is what is actually happening at each stage. The ages are averages across large groups of children, and a child a year either side of any of them is inside the ordinary range.

Two to four

Nothing here involves print, and all of it is reading. A child is building the spoken vocabulary that decoding will later have to attach to, and learning that language has parts: that words rhyme, that names start with sounds, that a song has beats you can clap. Being read to matters more at this stage than at any later one, and what matters about it is the talking around the book rather than the book itself.

A four-year-old who knows no letters and has a large spoken vocabulary is in a stronger position than one who knows all twenty-six and rarely talks.

Four to six

Letters arrive, and the useful part of them is sounds rather than names. A child who can sing the alphabet may still be unable to read sat, because naming letters and blending sounds are separate skills and only the second one reads.

This is also where the gap between children is widest and least meaningful. Some five-year-olds decode simple words. Others are still working on hearing that sun and sock begin the same way, which is the prerequisite, not a failure to reach the goal. Both are on the same road at different points.

Six to eight

For most children this is when decoding becomes reliable and then becomes fast enough to stop being the main event. The shift worth watching for is not accuracy but effort: a child who reads a page correctly while concentrating hard on every word has not yet freed up the capacity to think about what it means.

Fluency is what releases comprehension. It comes from volume, which is why the single best thing available at this stage is a large quantity of books a child finds easy.

Eight and beyond

Decoding is largely finished as a project. Everything after this is vocabulary and background knowledge, because a child understands a page about monsoons to the extent that they already know something about monsoons. Reading progress at ten looks like knowing more about the world, not like better technique.

What the school starting age tells you

Formal reading instruction begins at four or five in some countries and six or seven in others. Children in the later-starting systems are not behind at twelve. Where a curriculum draws its line is a fact about the curriculum, and it is not information about your particular child in October.

The useful question is not whether your child has started. It is whether they are moving, and whether books are still something they are willing to sit with.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for an assessment by someone who knows your child.
how-to-teach-a-child-to-read-at-home:
Almost everything that helps happens away from a reading lesson. What follows is a sequence rather than a list, because the steps depend on each other: doing step four before step two is the commonest way home reading practice goes wrong and ends in tears.

  1. Talk more than you teach. Reading attaches print to words a child already has. A word that is not in their ear cannot be decoded into meaning, only into noise. Narrate what you are doing, ask real questions, and let them finish their sentences without being corrected. This is the foundation and it never stops mattering.

  2. Play with sounds, with no print in sight. Rhyming, clapping syllables, spotting which words start the same, saying a word slowly and asking what it is. Five minutes in the car counts. This is the ability that reading research returns to most often as an early predictor, and it is entirely a listening skill.

  3. Read aloud, daily, above their level. Books they could not read themselves. This is where vocabulary and story structure come from, and it should continue for years after a child can read alone. Stopping read-aloud once a child decodes is the single most common mistake here.

  4. Teach letter sounds, not letter names. The sound the letter makes, lower case first, a few at a time, starting with ones that combine into real words: s, a, t, p, i, n. Twenty-six names learned in order is a song, not a tool.

  5. Blend, out loud, slowly. Say the sounds, then run them together. Sss-a-t. Sat. This is the moment reading actually begins, and for many children it needs weeks of patient repetition before it clicks. It will look like nothing is happening, and then it will happen.

  6. Give them books they find easy. Far too easy. A child who reads fifty simple books becomes fluent; a child who struggles through five hard ones learns that reading is where they fail. Volume at an easy level is what builds speed, and speed is what frees up the thinking.

  7. Keep the world coming in. Museums, cooking, questions about how things work, conversations about things that are not present. Comprehension at nine is mostly knowledge, and it is being built now.

How to handle a stuck moment

When a child stalls on a word, wait. Count to five silently. Most children get there, and the waiting is where the skill forms. If they do not, say the word and move on. Do not ask them to sound it out again, do not ask what letter it starts with, and do not turn one word into a two-minute lesson. The reading matters more than the word.

What to stop doing

Testing. Asking a child to read aloud to prove they can, correcting every error, and stopping to discuss mistakes are the three fastest routes to a child who avoids books. Aim for a child who reads badly and willingly rather than well and reluctantly. The first one becomes a reader.

When it is worth asking for help

If a child has had a year of instruction and blending still does not click, or if they can decode a word on one line and not the next, or if there is a family history of reading difficulty, it is worth raising with somebody who can assess directly. Support given early is lighter than support given at ten, and asking costs nothing.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for an assessment by someone who knows your child.
signs-your-child-is-ready-to-read:
Readiness is mostly audible rather than visible. The things worth noticing happen in conversation and play, not on a page, which is why parents watching for signs on paper often conclude there are none.

Here is what to listen and look for. Nobody has all of these at once, and they arrive in no fixed order.

In their ear

  • Notices when two words rhyme, or offers a rhyme unprompted
  • Can clap the beats in a word: ba-na-na
  • Spots that two words start with the same sound
  • Enjoys nonsense words and playing with how words sound
  • Can say what is left if you take the first sound off a word

Around print

  • Knows a book has a front, and which way the pages go
  • Understands that the marks carry the story, not the pictures
  • Points at words while being read to
  • Recognises their own name written down
  • Spots familiar signs and logos out of the house

In how they use language

  • Tells a story that has an order to it
  • Asks what words mean
  • Uses words they have only heard in books
  • Can follow a story with no pictures

In how they sit with it

  • Will stay with a book for several minutes
  • Comes back to the same book repeatedly
  • Chooses books when nobody has suggested it

What is not a sign

Knowing the alphabet song. Recognising letters by name. Age. Being able to write their name, which is a hand-control skill. Owning a lot of books. Having a sibling who read early.

None of these predict much. The sound-play ones at the top of this page predict a great deal, and they are the ones nobody thinks to look for.

If you are seeing very few

Then the useful work is the listening kind: rhymes, songs, clapping, silly words, being read to. That is the ground reading grows out of, and it is more productive than starting on letters with a child whose ear is not ready.
should-a-4-year-old-be-able-to-read:
No. And in most of the world nobody expects it, which is worth holding on to when a video of a fluent four-year-old turns up in your feed.

A small number of four-year-olds do read. They are not a benchmark. Some children assemble the pieces unusually early, in the same way some walk at nine months, and the research on early readers is consistently underwhelming about what it means later: by around eight or nine, the differences between early and typical readers have largely closed. Starting first is not the same as arriving further.

What a four-year-old should be doing is different in kind, not merely earlier on the same track. They are gathering the raw material: a spoken vocabulary that decoding will eventually attach to, an ear that can hear the parts inside words, the knowledge that print carries meaning, and the willingness to sit with a book. Every one of those is reading work. None of it looks like reading.

The thing most worth protecting at four is the appetite. A child who has learned that books are where the pressure lives has acquired something that takes years to undo, and it costs far more than a late start ever does. This is the actual risk at this age, and it is not the one parents are usually watching for.

So the honest answer to the question is that a four-year-old who is not reading is not behind, because there is nothing yet to be behind. If you want something to do about it, talk to them more, read to them daily, and play with sounds in the car. That is the whole programme, and it is more effective than any attempt to start early.

If your child is not putting sentences together, is not understanding what is said to them, or has had persistent ear infections, that is worth raising with someone who can assess directly. Those are hearing and language questions rather than reading ones, and they are worth answering early.
